Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge

Decouple applications with Amazon SQS queues, Amazon SNS topics, and Amazon EventBridge event buses.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

Serverless, Integration, and Event-Driven Design

Module 273, Serverless, Integration, and Event-Driven Design, covers serverless compute, application integration, and event-driven architectures on AWS. This lesson covers the three services that decouple applications: Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge.

Applications that call each other directly break together and slow down together. This lesson explains how Amazon SQS queues buffer work, how Amazon SNS topics fan out one message to many receivers, and how Amazon EventBridge routes events from AWS services, SaaS applications, and your own code. You then learn to choose and combine them. The last two tabs prepare you for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam.

The tabs in this lesson cover the following topics:

  • Tab 1: why decoupling matters, and the queue, publish/subscribe, and event bus models.
  • Tab 2: standard and FIFO queues, queue settings, the visibility timeout, long polling, delay queues, and dead-letter queues.
  • Tab 3: scaling consumers with Auto Scaling and Lambda, common patterns, security, and large messages.
  • Tab 4: topics and subscriptions, fan-out with SQS, message filtering, FIFO topics, and delivery.
  • Tab 5: event buses, rules and event patterns, targets, schedules, archive and replay, the schema registry, and Pipes.
  • Tab 6: choosing and combining SQS, SNS, and EventBridge, when to use Kinesis, and Amazon MQ for existing message brokers.
  • Tab 7: what you pay for and how to lower the cost.
  • Tab 8: the SAA-C03 cheat sheet, exam scenarios, and the lesson summary.
  • Tab 9: open-ended Knowledge Check questions with model answers.

Introduction

Every event-driven design depends on a reliable way to pass messages between its parts. Choosing between a queue, a topic, and an event bus, and setting them up correctly, decides whether a system survives a traffic spike or a failed component. These choices appear in many SAA-C03 questions.

This lesson follows FlashCart Inc. through the Problem Statement of each tab. It assumes Lesson 273.1, AWS Lambda, and Lesson 273.2, Amazon API Gateway.

Use the tab list on the left, or the Previous and Next buttons, to move through the lesson. Each topic tab opens with a Problem Statement and ends with exam traps, keyword triggers, and resource links. The Knowledge Check is the last tab.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

  1. Define queues, publish/subscribe, and event buses, and identify when to decouple applications.
  2. Implement SQS with dead-letter queues, long polling, and consumers that scale with Lambda or Auto Scaling.
  3. Apply SNS fan-out to SQS queues with message filtering.
  4. Use EventBridge rules, event patterns, schedules, and archive and replay to route events.
  5. Distinguish standard and FIFO queues, and select queue settings for a workload.
  6. Compare SQS, SNS, and EventBridge, and justify the choice for a scenario.
  7. Design a decoupled, event-driven architecture with SQS, SNS, and EventBridge.

1. Decoupling and Messaging Models

Problem Statement

FlashCart Inc. is an online retailer that handles about 2,000 orders an hour on a normal day and up to 40,000 an hour during a flash sale. In Lesson 273.1, the team moved the order API to AWS Lambda, but the order function still calls four services one after another before it answers the customer: payment, the email service of an outside vendor, analytics, and the warehouse system.

During the last flash sale, the email vendor slowed down and answered in 8 to 10 seconds instead of 200 milliseconds. Every order function waited for it, the API timed out, and about 6 percent of the orders failed. Some customers were charged but never saw a confirmation, and the analytics service dropped the events that arrived while it was overloaded.

The CTO sets three goals: the customer must get an order confirmation in under one second, a slow or failed downstream service must never lose or block an order, and the new loyalty team must be able to receive orders next month without any change to the order code.

Your challenge:

  • Decide which of the four calls must stay synchronous, and which can be handed off and processed later.
  • Choose the messaging model that fits each hand-off: a queue, publish/subscribe, or an event bus.
  • Explain how your design meets each of the CTO's three goals.

1.1 Why Decouple Applications

  • When applications call each other directly and wait (synchronous communication), a slow or failed receiver slows or breaks the caller.
  • A sudden spike is also a problem: if a system usually encodes 10 videos but must suddenly encode 1,000, a direct design overloads the receiver.
  • Decoupling puts a managed service in the middle. The sender hands off the work and moves on, and the receiver processes it at its own pace.
  • On AWS, three services decouple applications: Amazon SQS (queues), Amazon SNS (publish/subscribe), and Amazon EventBridge (event bus). They scale independently of your applications.

1.2 Three Messaging Models

ModelServiceHow it worksTypical use
QueueAmazon SQSProducers send messages to a queue. Consumers poll the queue, process each message, and delete it. Each message is processed by one consumer.Buffering work, absorbing spikes, and spreading tasks across workers.
Publish/subscribeAmazon SNSA publisher sends a message to a topic, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber of the topic.Sending one message to many receivers, notifications, and fan-out.
Event busAmazon EventBridgeEvent sources send events to a bus, and rules match each event by its content and route it to targets.Reacting to AWS service, SaaS, and custom events, and running schedules.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: An order service calls a slow email service directly, and during traffic spikes the orders time out. The company wants the order service to hand off the email work and continue, and the email service to process the work at its own pace. Which AWS service fits best?

  • A. An Application Load Balancer in front of the email service.
  • B. A larger EC2 instance for the email service.
  • C. Amazon SQS, with the email service polling a queue.
  • D. Amazon CloudFront.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. A queue decouples the two services: the order service sends a message and moves on, and the email service polls and processes the messages at its own pace, while the queue absorbs spikes.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA load balancer still calls the service synchronously.
BIncorrectA bigger server does not remove the synchronous dependency.
CCorrectThis is the standard decoupling pattern.
DIncorrectCloudFront caches content; it does not decouple services.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Decouple, buffer, absorb spikes = SQS. One message to many receivers = SNS. Route events by content, SaaS events, schedules = EventBridge.
  • SQS is pull (consumers poll). SNS and EventBridge push to their targets.

Memory Hook

Queue: one worker per message. Topic: everyone gets a copy. Bus: the rules decide.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

→ Amazon SQS

Trigger 2: "Send the same message to many services"
→ Amazon SNS

Trigger 3: "React to events from AWS services or SaaS apps"
→ Amazon EventBridge

2. Amazon SQS Fundamentals

Problem Statement

FlashCart creates an order-processing queue between the order API and a group of worker servers. Most orders take the workers 10 seconds to process, but large orders go through a fraud check that takes up to 3 minutes. Since the change, about 1 order in 200 is processed twice, and some customers received two shipping labels.

The invoicing team has a stricter need: for each customer account, a credit note must always be processed before the invoice that follows it, and an invoice must never be issued twice. A third team wants welcome-offer emails sent 10 minutes after a customer signs up, not at once.

Two more problems appear in the logs. An old version of the mobile app sends a malformed order message that fails every time, so it returns to the queue again and again and keeps workers busy for nothing. At night, when the queue is empty, the workers send thousands of receive requests every hour that return no messages.

Your challenge:

  • Explain why orders are processed twice, and choose the queue setting and the value that stop it.
  • Choose the queue type for the invoicing team, and explain how it keeps the order for each account and prevents duplicates.
  • Choose the settings for the welcome-offer delay, the malformed messages, and the empty receives at night.

2.1 How a Queue Works

  • Amazon SQS is a fully managed, highly available message queue. It stores messages until a consumer processes and deletes them.
  • Producers send messages with the SendMessage API. Consumers poll with ReceiveMessage, up to 10 messages at a time, process them, and then call DeleteMessage.
  • A message that is not deleted becomes visible again and can be processed again.
  • The number of messages that a queue can store is unlimited.

2.2 Standard and FIFO Queues

Standard queueFIFO queue
ThroughputNearly unlimited API calls per second.300 operations per second, or 3,000 messages per second with batching. High throughput mode supports up to 70,000 messages per second without batching.
DeliveryAt least once: a message can occasionally be delivered more than once.Exactly-once processing, with deduplication within a 5-minute interval.
OrderingBest effort: messages can arrive out of order.Strict first-in, first-out order within each message group (MessageGroupId).
NameAny queue name.The name must end with .fifo.
Use it forMost decoupling, where the consumer can handle a duplicate.Order-sensitive work, such as financial transactions or inventory updates.

2.3 Key Queue Settings

SettingRange and defaultWhat it does
Visibility timeout0 seconds to 12 hours. Default 30 seconds.Hides a received message from other consumers while one consumer processes it.
Message retention period1 minute to 14 days. Default 4 days.Deletes messages that stay in the queue longer than this.
Maximum message size1 KiB to 1,024 KiB (1 MiB). Default 1,024 KiB.Limits the size of each message.
Delivery delay0 seconds to 15 minutes. Default 0.Keeps new messages hidden for a time after they arrive (a delay queue).
Receive message wait time0 to 20 seconds. Default 0 (short polling).Any value above 0 turns on long polling.

2.4 Visibility Timeout

  • When a consumer receives a message, the message becomes invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout.
  • If the consumer deletes the message in time, it is gone. If not, the message becomes visible again and another consumer can process it, so it may be processed twice.
  • Set the timeout longer than the normal processing time. A consumer that needs more time can call the ChangeMessageVisibility API.
  • Too high: if a consumer crashes, the message waits a long time before a retry. Too low: messages are processed more than once.

2.5 Long Polling, Delay Queues, and Dead-Letter Queues

  • Long polling makes ReceiveMessage wait up to 20 seconds for a message to arrive, instead of returning at once with no messages. It reduces empty responses, the number of API calls, and the cost.
  • A delay queue keeps new messages hidden for 0 to 15 minutes. You can also delay one message with the DelaySeconds parameter.
  • A dead-letter queue (DLQ) receives the messages that fail too many times. You set the maximum receives (maxReceiveCount), for example 5. After that many receives without a delete, SQS moves the message to the DLQ.
  • A DLQ stops a bad ("poison") message from being retried forever and lets you investigate it. After you fix the problem, a redrive moves the messages back to the source queue.
  • The DLQ of a standard queue must be a standard queue, and the DLQ of a FIFO queue must be a FIFO queue.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: Consumers of a standard SQS queue take up to 3 minutes to process each message, and the team notices that some messages are processed twice. The queue uses the default settings. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

  • A. The visibility timeout of 30 seconds is shorter than the processing time. Increase it above 3 minutes.
  • B. The retention period is too short. Increase it to 14 days.
  • C. Long polling is off. Set the wait time to 20 seconds.
  • D. The queue is too small. Create a larger queue.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. With the default 30-second visibility timeout, a message becomes visible again while a consumer is still working on it, so another consumer receives it.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectThe timeout must be longer than the processing time.
BIncorrectRetention controls how long unprocessed messages are kept.
CIncorrectLong polling reduces empty responses, not duplicates.
DIncorrectA queue has no size to choose: storage is unlimited.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Duplicates with slow consumers = raise the visibility timeout, or call ChangeMessageVisibility.
  • Strict order or no duplicates = a FIFO queue, which ends in .fifo and is limited to 300 operations per second, or 3,000 messages per second with batching.
  • Too many empty receives and high API cost = long polling, with a wait time up to 20 seconds.
  • Poison messages = a dead-letter queue with a maximum receive count.
  • Messages are kept for 4 days by default and 14 days at most, and can be up to 1 MiB.

Memory Hook

Visibility hides, delay waits, long polling listens, and the DLQ catches the failures.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Messages must be processed in order with no duplicates"
→ SQS FIFO queue

Trigger 2: "Consumer takes longer than 30 seconds and messages repeat"
→ Increase the visibility timeout

Trigger 3: "Reduce empty responses and the cost of polling"
→ Long polling

Trigger 4: "Isolate messages that keep failing"
→ Dead-letter queue

3. Amazon SQS in Architectures

Problem Statement

The order queue works, but the flash sale exposes new limits. Within an hour, the backlog grows to 200,000 messages, and the two worker servers fall about six hours behind. During the rest of the day, the same two servers sit almost idle, and the finance team asks why FlashCart pays for them at night.

The developers want to move some consumers to AWS Lambda, but they worry about how a function would read the queue. In a test, one bad message in a batch of 10 made the function fail, and all 10 messages were processed again.

The security team adds requirements: order data must be encrypted at rest with a key that FlashCart controls, only the order service may send messages to the queue, and the worker servers run in private subnets with no internet access. The billing team also needs to pass invoice PDFs of up to 5 MB through the same flow.

Your challenge:

  • Design how the consumers scale with the backlog, both for EC2 workers and for Lambda.
  • Explain how to stop one bad message from making a whole batch run again.
  • Meet the security requirements for encryption, sending permissions, and private access.
  • Choose how the 5 MB invoice PDFs travel through the queue.

3.1 Scaling Consumers

  • EC2 Auto Scaling: a CloudWatch alarm on the queue length metric, ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, makes the Auto Scaling group add workers when the queue grows and remove them when it shrinks.
  • AWS Lambda: an event source mapping polls the queue for you and invokes the function with batches of messages. Lambda scales the number of concurrent functions with the queue depth, and deletes the messages after a successful batch.
  • The batch size is 10 messages by default. It can be up to 10,000 for a standard queue and 10 for a FIFO queue, with a batch window of up to 5 minutes.
  • With partial batch responses (batch item failures), the function reports only the failed messages, so the successful ones are not processed again.
  • Set the visibility timeout of the queue longer than the function timeout, so a message is not received again while the function still processes it.

Source Note

One course slide gives the Lambda batch size for SQS as 1 to 10. That is out of date: AWS now allows up to 10,000 messages per batch for standard queues, and 10 for FIFO queues.

3.2 Common Patterns

  • Buffer for database writes: the front end sends each write to a queue, and workers write to the database at a steady pace, so a spike does not overload the database or lose transactions.
  • Buffer for an API: API Gateway sends requests to a queue, and Lambda processes them, so a burst of requests waits in the queue.
  • Decouple application tiers: the front-end and back-end tiers each scale on their own, with a queue between them.

3.3 Security

  • In transit: all SQS API calls use HTTPS.
  • At rest: server-side encryption with SSE-SQS (keys managed by SQS) or SSE-KMS (a key in AWS KMS). Clients can also encrypt the messages themselves.
  • Access: IAM policies control who can call the SQS API. An SQS access policy on the queue, like an S3 bucket policy, allows access from other AWS accounts or lets SNS, S3, or EventBridge send messages to the queue.
  • Private access: an interface VPC endpoint lets instances in private subnets reach SQS without the internet (Lesson 269.3).

3.4 Large Messages

  • A message can be up to 1 MiB. AWS raised this quota from 256 KiB in 2025, so older material still says 256 KB.
  • For larger payloads, the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library (Java and Python) stores the payload in Amazon S3 and sends a reference to it in the message, for payloads up to 2 GB.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A worker fleet on EC2 processes messages from an SQS queue. During sales, the queue grows quickly and messages wait for hours. Which approach scales the fleet with the backlog?

  • A. A longer retention period.
  • B. A larger visibility timeout.
  • C. A FIFO queue instead of a standard queue.
  • D. A CloudWatch alarm on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric that drives an Auto Scaling policy for the worker group.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. The queue length shows the backlog. An alarm on it adds workers when the queue grows and removes them when it shrinks.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectRetention keeps messages longer; it does not process them faster.
BIncorrectThe visibility timeout does not add capacity.
CIncorrectA FIFO queue limits throughput.
DCorrectThis is the standard pattern for scaling consumers.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Scale EC2 workers on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible. Lambda scales automatically with the queue depth through an event source mapping.
  • Visibility timeout of the queue should be longer than the Lambda function timeout.
  • Messages larger than 1 MiB = the Extended Client Library with S3.
  • SNS or S3 cannot write to a queue unless the SQS access policy allows it.

Memory Hook

The queue length drives the workers, and S3 carries what does not fit.

4. Amazon SNS

Problem Statement

Each new order now goes into one queue, but four teams need it: payment, email, analytics, and the warehouse. With a single queue, each message reaches only one consumer, so the teams compete for the same messages, and some teams never see some orders.

The warehouse team wants only orders over 500 dollars, which need special packing, and does not want to read and discard every other order. The loyalty team will join next month, and the order team refuses to change its code again for a new consumer.

Other teams add their own needs. The operations team wants a text message (SMS) when a payment fails, and the customer service team wants a push notification sent to the mobile app. Some consumers go offline for maintenance for an hour at a time, and they must not lose orders while they are down. Refund events must reach the refund system in the order in which they happened, with no duplicates.

Your challenge:

  • Design how one order message reaches all four teams, each at its own pace, without loss.
  • Make sure that the warehouse receives only the large orders, and that the loyalty team can join without changes to the order service.
  • Choose how to deliver the SMS and mobile push notifications.
  • Keep the refund events in order with no duplicates.

4.1 What Amazon SNS Is

  • Amazon SNS is a managed publish/subscribe service. A publisher sends a message to a topic, and SNS delivers a copy to every subscriber.
  • It supports application-to-application (A2A) messaging, to SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S endpoints, and Amazon Data Firehose, and application-to-person (A2P) messaging, to email, SMS, and mobile push notifications.
  • SNS pushes the messages, and it does not keep them: a subscriber that is not available can miss a message unless retries or a dead-letter queue catch it.
  • Many AWS services publish to SNS, such as CloudWatch alarms, AWS Budgets, S3 events, and Auto Scaling notifications.
LimitStandard topicFIFO topic
Topics per account100,0001,000
Subscriptions per topic12,500,000100
Ordering and duplicatesBest-effort order, and a message can be delivered more than once.Strict order within a message group, and deduplication within 5 minutes.
SubscribersAll protocols.SQS queues.

4.2 Fan-Out With SNS and SQS

  • Fan-out means "send once, deliver to many". The publisher sends one message to an SNS topic, and each subscribed SQS queue receives a copy.
  • Each queue keeps its copy until its own consumer processes it, so the design is fully decoupled with no data loss, and each consumer can retry, delay, and scale on its own.
  • You can add a new subscriber later without changing the publisher.
  • The SQS access policy of each queue must allow the SNS topic to send messages to it. Queues in other Regions can subscribe too.
  • S3 events to many targets: S3 allows only one event notification for the same event type and prefix, so send it to an SNS topic and fan out to several queues or functions. You can also send S3 events to EventBridge.
  • SNS FIFO topics with SQS FIFO queues give fan-out with ordering and deduplication.

4.3 Message Filtering

  • By default, every subscriber receives every message of the topic.
  • A filter policy on a subscription is a JSON document that tells SNS which messages to deliver to that subscriber, based on the message attributes or the message body.
  • For example, the warehouse queue receives only messages where eventType is "OrderCreated" and the amount is above a value, and the support queue receives only low-priority issues.
  • Filtering removes the work of discarding unwanted messages in each consumer. A topic can have up to 200 filter policies.

4.4 Delivery, Security, and Large Messages

  • SNS retries deliveries that fail. AWS recommends a dead-letter queue (an SQS queue) on every subscription, to capture the messages that cannot be delivered.
  • Security: HTTPS in transit, encryption at rest with AWS KMS, IAM policies, and an SNS access policy on the topic, for example to let another account or an S3 bucket publish.
  • Message size: 256 KiB by default. You can raise it up to 1 MiB with the MaximumMessageSize topic attribute, for topics with SQS, Lambda, and Firehose subscribers only, up to 100 subscriptions. The SNS Extended Client Library stores larger payloads, up to 2 GB, in S3.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: An order service must send each order to a payment service, a shipping service, and a fraud service. Each service must process every order at its own pace, and new services will be added later without changes to the order service. Which design fits best?

  • A. Send each order to one SQS queue read by all three services.
  • B. Publish each order to an SNS topic, and subscribe one SQS queue per service.
  • C. Call the three services directly from the order service.
  • D. Write each order to an S3 bucket and let the services list the bucket.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: B. SNS and SQS fan-out delivers a copy of each order to each queue, so every service processes every order at its own pace, and new queues can subscribe later.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectIn one queue, each message is processed by only one consumer.
BCorrectThis is the fan-out pattern.
CIncorrectDirect calls are tightly coupled.
DIncorrectListing a bucket is not a messaging design.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Every service must get every message = SNS fan-out to SQS, not one shared queue.
  • Only some messages to a subscriber = a filter policy on the subscription.
  • Fan-out with order and no duplicates = SNS FIFO topic with SQS FIFO queues.
  • The queue needs an SQS access policy that allows the topic to send to it.

Memory Hook

Publish once, subscribe many, and filter what each one needs.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Send one message to several systems that each process it"
→ SNS topic with SQS subscriptions (fan-out)

Trigger 2: "Subscriber needs only some of the messages"
→ SNS subscription filter policy

Trigger 3: "Same S3 event to several queues"
→ S3 event notification to SNS, then fan-out

Trigger 4: "Email or SMS notification from an application"
→ Amazon SNS

5. Amazon EventBridge

Problem Statement

FlashCart now has events from many places that it must react to. AWS services produce some of them: an EC2 instance stops unexpectedly, or a file arrives in an S3 bucket. The SaaS help desk produces others: a customer opens a support ticket about a refund. FlashCart's own services publish the rest, such as "order shipped".

Today, three EC2 servers do nothing but run cron jobs: a nightly cleanup, an hourly price sync, and a weekly report. They cost money all day and fail silently when a server stops. The security team also wants the security findings from all 12 FlashCart AWS accounts collected in one central account.

Last week, a bug in the shipping consumer processed every "order shipped" event wrongly for two days. The bug is fixed, but those events are gone, and the team has no way to process them again. New developers also keep asking what fields each event contains.

Your challenge:

  • Choose how to receive and route the AWS, SaaS, and custom events, each to the right targets.
  • Replace the three cron servers with a serverless schedule.
  • Collect the events of all 12 accounts in one central account.
  • Make it possible to replay past events, and give developers a reliable description of each event.

5.1 What Amazon EventBridge Is

  • Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, SaaS applications, and your own applications to targets, using rules.
  • An event is a JSON object that describes a change, with fields such as source, detail-type, and detail.
  • It replaces point-to-point integrations: sources do not need to know the targets.
  • It was formerly called Amazon CloudWatch Events.

5.2 Event Buses

Event busWhat it receives
Default event busCreated automatically in every account. Receives events from AWS services.
Partner event busReceives events from integrated SaaS partners, such as Zendesk or Datadog, without webhooks.
Custom event busReceives events from your own applications, and events shared from other accounts.
  • A resource-based policy on a bus lets other AWS accounts or Regions send events to it, for example to collect the events of all the accounts in an AWS Organization in one account.
  • An event can be up to 1 MB. AWS raised this from 256 KB in January 2026, in most commercial Regions, so older material still says 256 KB.

5.3 Rules, Event Patterns, and Targets

  • A rule matches incoming events with an event pattern and sends the matching events to up to 5 targets, such as Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, Kinesis, API Gateway, or another event bus.
  • Patterns can match exact values, prefixes, numeric ranges, and "anything-but" values.
  • An input transformer can change the event before it reaches the target.
  • If a target fails, EventBridge retries the delivery, by default for up to 24 hours and 185 attempts. Configure an SQS dead-letter queue on the target to keep the events that still fail.
  • A bus has up to 300 rules by default, and the quota can be raised.
{
  "source": ["aws.ec2"],
  "detail-type": ["EC2 Instance State-change Notification"],
  "detail": { "state": ["stopped"] }
}

This event pattern matches the events sent when any EC2 instance in the account stops. A rule with this pattern and an SNS topic as its target notifies the operations team.

5.4 Schedules, Archive and Replay, Schema Registry, and Pipes

  • Schedules: run a target on a cron or rate expression, like a serverless cron job. EventBridge Scheduler is the separate feature recommended for new schedules, including one-time schedules.
  • Archive and replay: an archive keeps a copy of the events on a bus, all of them or the ones that match a pattern, indefinitely or for a period that you set. You can replay archived events later, for example after a consumer bug is fixed.
  • Schema Registry: EventBridge can discover the structure of the events on a bus and store it as a schema, and you can generate code bindings from it.
  • EventBridge Pipes: a point-to-point integration from one source, such as an SQS queue, a Kinesis stream, or DynamoDB Streams, through optional filtering and enrichment, to one target.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: An operations team must be notified whenever any EC2 instance in the account stops, with the least operational overhead. What should a solutions architect configure?

  • A. An SQS queue that the instances write to before they stop.
  • B. A Lambda function that lists all instances every minute.
  • C. An EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches EC2 state-change events with the state stopped, with an SNS topic as the target.
  • D. A CloudTrail trail with an S3 bucket.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. EC2 sends state-change events to the default event bus, and a rule with a pattern routes the matching events to an SNS topic, with no code to run.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectInstances do not reliably send messages when they stop.
BIncorrectPolling adds code, cost, and delay.
CCorrectThis is the native, event-driven solution.
DIncorrectCloudTrail records API calls, but it does not notify by itself.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • React to AWS service events or SaaS events, or run on a schedule = EventBridge.
  • A rule has up to 5 targets. For more receivers, target an SNS topic and fan out.
  • Replay past events = archive and replay. Events from other accounts = a resource-based policy on the bus.
  • EventBridge was formerly CloudWatch Events.

Memory Hook

6. Choosing the Right Service

Problem Statement

The FlashCart architecture review board meets every week, and the same argument keeps coming back: SQS, SNS, and EventBridge all "move messages", so which one should each new feature use? This week, four features are on the agenda.

Feature 1 resizes product images: each upload creates a job that takes about 30 seconds, and uploads arrive in bursts. Feature 2 announces price changes: six teams must each receive every change. Feature 3 reacts to disputes raised in the SaaS payment platform, and routes them by country and amount. Feature 4 collects website clickstream data, about 50,000 events per second, that three analytics teams must each read in order and be able to read again. Feature 5 moves the warehouse system from the FlashCart data center to AWS: it already exchanges messages through a RabbitMQ broker, using the AMQP protocol, and the warehouse team has no budget to rewrite it.

Your challenge:

  • Choose a service, or a combination of services, for each of the five features.
  • Justify each choice with the delivery model, how the messages are kept, and the filtering that the feature needs.
  • Identify the two features for which none of the three messaging services is the best fit, and name the better option for each.

6.1 Choosing Between SQS, SNS, and EventBridge

Amazon SQSAmazon SNSAmazon EventBridge
ModelQueue (pull).Publish/subscribe (push).Event bus with rules (push).
ReceiversOne consumer per message.Every subscriber gets a copy.Up to 5 targets per rule, chosen by content.
Keeps messagesYes, 1 minute to 14 days.No. Retries, then a DLQ.No, unless you archive them.
FilteringNo. Consumers read every message.Filter policies on subscriptions.Event patterns on rules.
SourcesYour applications, and SNS, S3, or EventBridge.Your applications and many AWS services.AWS services, SaaS partners, your applications, and schedules.
Best forBuffering and spreading work.Fan-out and notifications to people.Routing events across services and accounts.

6.2 Combining the Services

  • SNS plus SQS: fan-out, where each consumer keeps its own copy in a queue.
  • EventBridge plus SQS: a rule sends matching events to a queue, so a consumer can process them at its own pace.
  • EventBridge plus SNS: a rule sends events to a topic to reach more than 5 receivers or people.
  • Ordered work: SQS FIFO queues, alone or behind an SNS FIFO topic.

6.3 When to Use Kinesis Instead

  • Amazon Kinesis Data Streams keeps an ordered stream of records for a set time, and several applications can read the same records, and read them again.
  • Use it for real-time analytics of large data streams, such as clickstreams, logs, or IoT data, where many consumers read the same data in order.
  • Use SQS, SNS, or EventBridge for application messages and events. Kinesis is covered with the streaming services.

6.4 Amazon MQ for Existing Message Brokers

  • SQS and SNS are cloud-native services with their own AWS APIs. Many applications that run on premises use a traditional message broker, such as Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ, with open messaging APIs and protocols.
  • Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service for ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ. When you migrate such an application to AWS, Amazon MQ lets it keep its broker, APIs, and protocols, instead of re-engineering it to use SQS and SNS.
  • It supports industry-standard APIs and protocols: JMS, NMS, AMQP 0-9-1 and 1.0, STOMP, MQTT, OpenWire, and WebSocket.
  • It has both queues (point-to-point) and topics (publish/subscribe).
  • Amazon MQ manages the broker nodes, applies patches, replicates data for high availability, and supports engine version upgrades.
  • Unlike SQS and SNS, it is not serverless: it runs on broker instances whose type you choose, so it does not scale as much as SQS and SNS.
Deployment modeEngineHow it works
Single-instance brokerActiveMQ and RabbitMQOne broker. Recommended for evaluation and testing: if it fails, it is unavailable until it restarts.
Active/standby brokerActiveMQTwo brokers in two Availability Zones, with shared storage in Amazon EFS. If the active broker or its zone fails, the standby takes over.
Cluster deploymentRabbitMQThree nodes across Availability Zones, backed by Amazon EBS, with replication for high availability.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company needs to route events from its SaaS help desk and from AWS services to different Lambda functions, based on fields inside each event, with no custom polling code. Which service fits best?

  • A. Amazon EventBridge with rules and event patterns.
  • B. Amazon SQS standard queue.
  • C. Amazon SNS topic without filters.
  • D. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. EventBridge receives events from SaaS partners and AWS services, and its rules route each event to targets by matching fields in the event.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectIt routes by content from many sources.
BIncorrectA queue does not route by content, and SaaS apps do not write to it natively.
CIncorrectWithout filters, every subscriber gets every message.
DIncorrectKinesis is for streaming data, not event routing.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Buffer = SQS. Fan-out = SNS. Route by content, SaaS, schedule = EventBridge. Replayable ordered stream, many readers = Kinesis.
  • SNS does not keep messages. Put an SQS queue behind it when a consumer must not lose messages.
  • Migrate an application that uses RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, or protocols such as AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, or JMS, without rewriting it = Amazon MQ, not SQS or SNS.
  • For a highly available Amazon MQ broker, use active/standby (ActiveMQ) or a cluster (RabbitMQ) across Availability Zones.

Memory Hook

Wait in line: SQS. Tell everyone: SNS. Send it to the right place: EventBridge.

→ SQS

Trigger 2: "Tell many systems at once"
→ SNS

Trigger 3: "Route events by their content, from AWS and SaaS"
→ EventBridge

Trigger 4: "Many consumers read the same ordered stream, with replay"
→ Kinesis Data Streams

Trigger 5: "Move an on-premises RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ application without code changes"
→ Amazon MQ

7. Pricing

Problem Statement

Three months after the redesign, the FlashCart monthly bill for messaging is three times higher than the team expected. The finance team asks how SQS, SNS, and EventBridge are billed, and why the bill grew so much.

An investigation finds three causes. The workers short-poll the queues all night, which creates millions of receive requests that return no messages. The order service sends each message in a separate request instead of in batches. Every Lambda subscriber of the order topic is invoked for every order, then discards about 80 percent of them in code. The team has also archived every event on every bus, including events that nobody will ever replay.

Your challenge:

  • Explain what each of the three services charges for.
  • Match each cause in the investigation to a fix that lowers the bill without slowing down the orders.
  • Decide which events are worth archiving.

7.1 What You Pay For

ServiceMain cost drivers
Amazon SQSThe number of requests (send, receive, and delete). FIFO requests cost more than standard requests. Each 64 KB chunk of a payload counts as one request.
Amazon SNSThe number of messages published, and the deliveries by protocol. SMS and mobile push are priced separately.
Amazon EventBridgeCustom, partner, and cross-account events, archive storage, replays, Pipes requests, and Scheduler invocations. Events from AWS services to the default bus are free.
All threeData transfer, and the AWS KMS requests when you use a KMS key.

7.2 Lowering the Cost

  • Use long polling in SQS to remove empty receive requests.
  • Use batch APIs to send, receive, and delete up to 10 messages per request.
  • Use filter policies and event patterns, so consumers and functions run only for the messages they need.
  • Archive only the events that you need to replay.
  • Check the SQS, SNS, and EventBridge pricing pages for the current prices.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: An SQS consumer polls a quiet queue in a tight loop, and most receive requests return no messages. How can the team lower the SQS cost without delaying messages?

  • A. Increase the retention period.
  • B. Increase the visibility timeout.
  • C. Use a FIFO queue.
  • D. Set the receive message wait time to 20 seconds to use long polling.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. Long polling waits for messages to arrive, so the consumer sends far fewer empty receive requests, and messages are still returned as soon as they arrive.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectRetention does not affect polling.
BIncorrectIt does not change how often the consumer polls.
CIncorrectFIFO requests cost more.
DCorrectIt removes empty responses.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Many empty receives = turn on long polling.

Memory Hook

Pay per request: poll long, batch big, and filter early.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Lower SQS request cost on a quiet queue"
→ Long polling

Trigger 2: "Fewer API calls for many messages"
→ Batch APIs

8.2 Exam Scenarios

Scenario 1

Scenario: A video platform uploads files to S3 and must create thumbnails, extract metadata, and scan for malware, each with its own Lambda function, and each function must retry on its own when it fails.

Show Answer and Explanation

Answer: Send the S3 event to an SNS topic (or to EventBridge) and fan out to one SQS queue per function, each with a dead-letter queue. S3 allows only one notification per event type and prefix, and the queues let each function retry and scale on its own.

Scenario 2

Scenario: A bank must process account transactions in the exact order they happen, for each account, with no duplicates, at about 1,000 transactions per second.

Show Answer and Explanation

Answer: An SQS FIFO queue, with the account ID as the message group ID. FIFO keeps the order within each group and removes duplicates. With batching, a FIFO queue supports 3,000 messages per second, and high throughput mode supports more.

Scenario 3

Scenario: A company wants all security findings and CloudTrail events from its 40 AWS accounts in one central account, where rules route them to a ticketing system.

Show Answer and Explanation

Answer: In each account, an EventBridge rule sends the events to a custom event bus in the central account, whose resource-based policy allows the organization to send events. Rules on the central bus route the events to the ticketing system.

8.3 Lesson Summary

This lesson covered the following points:

  • SQS, SNS, and EventBridge decouple applications with three models: a queue, publish/subscribe, and an event bus.
  • SQS standard queues give nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery, and FIFO queues give strict order and deduplication. The visibility timeout, retention, delay, long polling, and dead-letter queues control how messages are processed.
  • Consumers scale with the queue: EC2 Auto Scaling on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, or Lambda event source mappings. Messages can be up to 1 MiB, and larger payloads go to S3 with the Extended Client Library.
  • SNS pushes one message to many subscribers. SNS and SQS fan-out decouples every consumer, filter policies send each subscriber only what it needs, and FIFO topics keep the order.
  • EventBridge routes AWS, SaaS, and custom events with rules and patterns to up to 5 targets per rule, and adds schedules, archive and replay, a schema registry, Pipes, and cross-account buses.
  • Amazon MQ is the managed ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ broker for applications that use open messaging protocols and must move to AWS without a rewrite.

Memory Hook

SQS waits, SNS tells, EventBridge routes.

9. Knowledge Check

Answer each question in your own words before you open the model answer.

Question 1: Compare the queue, publish/subscribe, and event bus models, and name the AWS service for each.

Maps to: Objective 1 (Comprehension).

In a queue (Amazon SQS), producers send messages, and consumers poll, process, and delete them, so each message is processed by one consumer. In publish/subscribe (Amazon SNS), a publisher sends a message to a topic, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber. In an event bus (Amazon EventBridge), sources send events to a bus, and rules match each event by its content and route it to targets. All three decouple the sender from the receivers.

Question 2: Distinguish standard and FIFO queues, and explain when to choose each.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Analysis).

Standard queues give nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, so consumers must handle an occasional duplicate. FIFO queues give strict order within a message group and exactly-once processing with deduplication within 5 minutes, at 300 operations per second, or 3,000 messages per second with batching, and the queue name ends in .fifo. Choose FIFO for order-sensitive work, such as transactions, and standard for most other decoupling.

Question 3: Explain the visibility timeout, long polling, delay queues, and dead-letter queues, and the problem each one solves.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Application).

The visibility timeout hides a received message from other consumers while one consumer processes it, from 0 seconds to 12 hours, 30 seconds by default. If it is too short, messages are processed twice. Long polling waits up to 20 seconds for messages, which removes empty responses and lowers the cost. A delay queue hides new messages for up to 15 minutes. A dead-letter queue receives the messages that exceed the maximum receive count, so a poison message does not block the queue, and a redrive moves them back after a fix.

Question 4: Describe two ways to scale the consumers of an SQS queue with the backlog.

Maps to: Objective 2 (Application).

For EC2 workers, a CloudWatch alarm on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric drives an Auto Scaling policy that adds workers when the queue grows and removes them when it shrinks. For Lambda, an event source mapping polls the queue, invokes the function with batches of up to 10,000 messages for standard queues, scales the concurrency with the queue depth, and deletes the messages after success, with partial batch responses to retry only the failed messages.

Question 5: Explain the SNS and SQS fan-out pattern and how filter policies change it.

Maps to: Objective 3 (Application).

The publisher sends one message to an SNS topic, and every subscribed SQS queue receives a copy, so each consumer processes every message at its own pace, retries on its own, and new queues can subscribe without changing the publisher. The queues need access policies that allow the topic to send to them. A filter policy on a subscription makes SNS deliver only the matching messages to that queue, so each consumer receives only what it needs.

Question 6: Explain how EventBridge rules, event buses, schedules, and archive and replay work.

Maps to: Objective 4 (Application).

Events from AWS services arrive on the default bus, events from SaaS partners on partner buses, and events from your applications or other accounts on custom buses. A rule matches events with an event pattern and sends them to up to 5 targets, with retries and an optional dead-letter queue. Schedules run targets on a cron or rate expression, and EventBridge Scheduler is recommended for new schedules. An archive keeps a copy of the events on a bus, and you can replay them later, for example after fixing a bug.

Question 7: Design the order event flow for FlashCart: the order service publishes once, the payment, email, and analytics consumers each process every order at their own pace, the warehouse receives only large orders, a nightly cleanup runs without servers, and failed messages are kept.

Maps to: Objective 7 (Synthesis).

Publish each order to an SNS topic and subscribe one SQS queue per consumer, each with a dead-letter queue and an access policy for the topic. Add a filter policy to the warehouse subscription so it receives only orders above the value. Let Lambda event source mappings process the queues, with the queue visibility timeout longer than the function timeout and partial batch responses. Use an SQS FIFO queue, or an SNS FIFO topic with FIFO queues, for any consumer that needs strict order. Run the nightly cleanup with EventBridge Scheduler, and send AWS service events, such as EC2 state changes, through EventBridge rules to SNS for the operations team.
